DSEM-CTX-G2.title: Research summary: SMS reminders and clinic attendance, Marlow District pilot
DSEM-CTX-G2.text:
Research Summary: Timed SMS Reminders and Outpatient Attendance
Marlow District Pilot, 2025 - summary prepared for the Health Services Research seminar
Authors: T. Brannigan (presenting), A. Idowu, M. Castellanos-Reyes

Background
Missed outpatient appointments in Marlow District ran at roughly 28% in 2024. We tested whether two timed text reminders improve attendance.

Design
Cluster-randomised trial across 14 clinics: 7 intervention, 7 control. Clinics volunteered in response to a district-wide invitation; of the 31 district clinics invited, 14 agreed. Randomisation was at clinic level, stratified by clinic size. Over a 12-week period the trial covered 2,406 scheduled appointments among 1,184 patients (1,221 appointments in intervention clinics, 1,185 in control clinics). Clinic staff and patients were not blinded to allocation.

Intervention clinics sent an SMS reminder 48 hours before the appointment and a second SMS 3 hours before. Control clinics continued usual practice (no reminder). Both reminders were always sent together, so the design cannot separate the effect of the 48-hour reminder from the 3-hour reminder.

Outcomes and analysis
The primary outcome was attendance at the scheduled appointment. The secondary outcome was late cancellation (less than 24 hours notice). Clinical health outcomes were not measured.

Analysis was intention-to-treat using mixed-effects logistic regression with a clinic random intercept, adjusting for age band, sex and appointment type. We used a random intercept because appointments within the same clinic are correlated; a simple chi-square test would treat all 2,406 appointments as independent and overstate precision. Appointments with a missing outcome (3.2%) were excluded (complete-case analysis).

Results
- Attendance: 78.4% in intervention clinics versus 71.9% in control clinics.
- Adjusted odds ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.77).
- Late cancellations fell from 9.3% (control) to 7.1% (intervention).
- Patients aged 65 and over: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.47), not significant. This subgroup contributed 412 appointments, and the trial was not powered for subgroup analysis.
- Delivery: 5,120 messages were sent; 6% were undeliverable (invalid or inactive numbers).
- Cost: each SMS cost 0.04 per message under the district's bulk contract.

Interpretation
Two timed reminders were associated with a 6.5 percentage point increase in attendance. Because only 14 clinics were randomised, the confidence interval is wide despite the number of appointments. The weaker estimate in older patients may reflect lower mobile phone use or simply the small subgroup; the data cannot distinguish these.

Limitations
- Short follow-up: 12-week duration, so we cannot say whether the effect persists or fades.
- Volunteer clinics may be more organised or motivated than those that declined.
- No blinding of clinic staff.
- 6% of messages were undeliverable and phone number accuracy was not audited.
- Results were not stratified by income or employment.
- We did not conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis.

Next steps
A follow-on trial would randomise from all 31 district clinics, run for 12 months, and test the 48-hour and 3-hour reminders as separate arms.

DSEM-CTX-G1.title: Thesis chapter 5: STAGE-KD keyword spotting results
DSEM-CTX-G1.text:
Chapter 5: Results and Discussion
Thesis: Staged Knowledge Distillation for Always-On Keyword Spotting on Microcontrollers
Candidate: R. Okonkwo-Hale, Department of Electrical Engineering, Veldmoor University (examination copy, final version)

5.1 Experimental setup
The teacher network, KWS-Large, has 18.4M parameters. The student, KWS-Tiny, has 212k parameters and is the model deployed on device. All models were trained on the Corvid Commands v2 corpus: 41,300 one-second utterances covering 35 keywords from 1,912 speakers. The test split contains 6,120 utterances from 288 held-out speakers who do not appear in training or validation.

We compare three ways of training KWS-Tiny: (a) training from scratch with cross-entropy, (b) standard KD, i.e. single-stage logit matching with temperature 4, and (c) STAGE-KD, our three-stage method. STAGE-KD runs logit matching first, then aligns intermediate features at student layers 3 and 6 with teacher layers 8 and 16, and finally fine-tunes for 2 epochs on hard labels with label smoothing of 0.1. Every configuration in Table 5.1 was trained with 5 random seeds; we report mean and standard deviation.

On-device numbers were measured on an Arlo M4 development board running at 80 MHz. Latency is measured per 1-second window, from feature input to posterior output; front-end feature extraction (40-band log-mel) was not timed separately.

5.2 Main results
Table 5.1 (test accuracy, mean +/- s.d. over 5 seeds):
- Scratch: 89.7% +/- 0.6
- Standard KD: 91.8% +/- 0.4
- STAGE-KD: 93.2% +/- 0.3
- Teacher (KWS-Large, reference only): 95.9%

STAGE-KD closes roughly a third of the gap between standard KD and the teacher. At the operating point of 1 false accept per hour, the false reject rate is 6.8% for STAGE-KD versus 9.4% for standard KD.

On the Arlo M4, KWS-Tiny runs in 14.2 ms per window with a peak RAM of 96 KB. Because all three training methods produce the same architecture, latency and memory are identical across them. We report latency only; energy per inference was not measured, as the board lacks a current-sense header.

5.3 Significance
We compared STAGE-KD against standard KD with a paired bootstrap over test utterances (10,000 resamples), pooling the predictions of the five seeds. We chose this over a t-test across seeds because five seeds give too few samples for a seed-level test to be informative. The difference is significant (p < 0.01). The bootstrap tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons across the ablation variants.

5.4 Ablations
Ablations used 3 seeds only, due to compute limits. Removing stage 2 (feature alignment) lowers accuracy to 92.0%; removing stage 3 (hard-label fine-tuning) lowers it to 92.9%. We read this as stage 2 contributing most of the gain, but the ablation differences are small relative to seed variance and should be treated as indicative.

5.5 Noise robustness
Under babble noise at 0 dB SNR, STAGE-KD reaches 71.5% and standard KD 70.9%. This gap is within seed variance, and we make no claim that STAGE-KD improves noise robustness.

5.6 Limitations
- English only; 71% of speakers self-reported US English, so accent coverage is skewed.
- One microcontroller (Arlo M4); results may not transfer to other boards or clock speeds.
- No energy measurements; latency is used as a proxy for cost.
- Near-field recordings only; nothing was tested beyond 1.5 m.
- Five seeds limit how precisely we can estimate variance, and the ablations use three.
- Baselines are limited to scratch training and standard KD.

5.7 Summary
STAGE-KD improves a 212k-parameter keyword spotter by 1.4 points over standard KD at no on-device cost, because the deployed architecture is unchanged. Future work: multilingual data, energy profiling, and far-field evaluation.

DSEM-CTX-I1.title: Seminar series logistics notes
DSEM-CTX-I1.text:
Department of Applied Sciences - Spring seminar series: logistics notes

Room: Lecture Theatre B2 (capacity 60). The projector takes HDMI; bring a USB-C adapter if your laptop needs one. The lectern microphone is wireless and runs on AA batteries; spares are in the top drawer of the lectern.

Timing: each slot is 40 minutes, split into 25 minutes of presentation and 15 minutes of questions. The chair shows a 5-minute and a 1-minute warning card. Please do not run into the next speaker's slot.

Catering: coffee and pastries at 10:30 in the foyer. Lunch orders must reach the department office by Tuesday noon. Dietary requirements go to the office, not to the caterer directly.

Recording: sessions are recorded only if every presenter in the slot consents in writing beforehand. Recordings are stored on the department drive for 90 days and then deleted.

Parking: visitor permits are available from reception; the east car park closes at 18:00.

Accessibility: step-free access via the north entrance; a hearing loop is available on request.

Questions about the series go to the seminar coordinator, room 3.14.

STAGE-KD for keyword spotting on microcontrollers

STAGE-KD reaches 94.1% test accuracy with a 212k-parameter student, averaged over five seeds, and runs in 11.8 ms on the Arlo M4 with 96 KB peak RAM. The improvement over standard KD is 2.5 points.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Let me push on the design. The clinics volunteered, didn't they? So you've got the keen ones in both arms, the staff knew which arm they were in, and nobody was blinded. How much of that six and a half point gap do you actually trust?
items.answer: You're right that the design has real limits, and the summary says so: clinics volunteered, staff and patients weren't blinded, and only 14 clinics were randomised. So I'd treat the 6.5 points as the estimate from this pilot, not a clean causal effect. The adjusted odds ratio was 1.41, with a wide confidence interval, 1.12 to 1.77, and the next step is randomising from all 31 district clinics.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Why not?
conversation: EXAMINER (heard): What's the latency on the device?

NATIVELY: On the Arlo M4, KWS-Tiny runs in **14.2 ms per window**, with a peak RAM of 96 KB. That's measured per 1-second window, from feature input to posterior output, so it excludes the front-end 40-band log-mel extraction, which wasn't timed separately. And since all three training methods produce the same architecture, latency is identical across them.
EXAMINER (heard): Does that include the feature extraction?

NATIVELY: No, it doesn't. Section 5.1 states latency is measured from feature input to posterior output, and the front-end 40-band log-mel extraction was not timed separately. So the 14.2 ms excludes it.
items.answer: Section 5.1 doesn't give a reason. It just states the measurement convention: latency is measured per 1-second window, from feature input to posterior output, and the 40-band log-mel front end wasn't timed separately. So the scope is the model itself, not the full pipeline. If you want the end-to-end number including the front end, that isn't in the chapter.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: So with fourteen hundred patients, why is the confidence interval on your odds ratio still that wide?
conversation: EXAMINER: Okay, thanks. I noted from your opening that it was about fourteen hundred patients across the district.
items.answer: The interval is wide because the unit of randomisation was the clinic, not the patient. Only 14 clinics were randomised, 7 intervention and 7 control, so the effective sample size is much closer to 14 than to the 2,406 appointments. Appointments within a clinic are correlated, which is why we used a mixed-effects model with a clinic random intercept rather than treating every appointment as independent. So the adjusted odds ratio is 1.41 with a 95% CI of 1.12 to 1.77, and that width reflects the small number of clusters, not the number of patients.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: examiner says my ablation is underpowered. draft something I can say out loud, honest but not defensive
items.answer: You're right that the ablation is underpowered, and I say so in the thesis. The ablations used three seeds because of compute limits, and the differences are small relative to seed variance, so I present them as indicative rather than conclusive. The main comparison is better supported: STAGE-KD against standard KD with a paired bootstrap over test utterances, 10,000 resamples, pooling five seeds, significant at p < 0.01. What I'd want to confirm is whether the concern is the seed count specifically or the lack of multiple-comparison correction across the ablation variants, since that's a separate gap I flag in the limitations.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: So basically you found that the feature alignment stage is what makes it work.
items.answer: Yes, with a caveat I want to be upfront about. In the ablations, removing stage 2 drops accuracy to 92.0% and removing stage 3 drops it to 92.9%, so stage 2 accounts for more of the gain. But those ablations used only 3 seeds, and the differences are small relative to seed variance, so I treat that as indicative rather than a firm claim.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What was the energy cost per inference on the microcontroller?
items.answer: Energy per inference wasn't measured, so I can't give you a number. The Arlo M4 board doesn't have a current-sense header, so I reported latency instead, 14.2 ms per one-second window, and used that as the proxy for cost. Energy profiling is listed as future work.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: For the non-specialists in the room, what is knowledge distillation, in a sentence or two?
items.answer:
Knowledge distillation is when a smaller model is trained to imitate the outputs of a larger, more capable one, so it picks up much of the same behaviour at a fraction of the size and cost. The big model acts as a teacher, and the small one learns from its soft predictions rather than only from hard labels.

That's the general definition, not something from the seminar logistics notes.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Could you explain what a confidence interval actually means? I always get it muddled.
items.answer: A 95% confidence interval means that if you repeated the same sampling procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals you built would contain the true value. It's a statement about the long-run behavior of the method, not a 95% probability that the true value sits inside this particular interval. The common mix-up is treating it as a probability about the parameter, when it's really about the procedure.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: if someone asks me something I genuinely don't know, how do I say that without sounding weak? also is it okay to say let's take it offline, and how do I stop myself rambling when I'm nervous
items.answer:
If I don't know something, I say so plainly and then say what I'll do about it: "I don't have that in front of me. Let me check and come back to you today." That reads as confidence, not weakness, because I'm owning the gap and the next step instead of guessing.

Taking it offline is fine when the detail is narrow or only matters to one or two people. If it's something the whole room needs, I answer what I can now and park the rest.

For rambling, I pause before I start, give the one-sentence answer first, then stop. If I feel myself drifting, I land the point and ask if that covers it.

conversation: EXAMINER (heard): What's the peak RAM on the board?

NATIVELY: The draft reports two different figures, so it depends which one you mean. Section 5.2 gives **112 KB** peak RAM, measured with the debug logger enabled. The summary paragraph carried over from the proposal says **96 KB** on the Arlo M4. There's a note to self in 5.5 about re-measuring the RAM figure with logging off, so the 112 KB may not be the final number.
items.answer: The table in 5.2 is the measured one: **112 KB** peak, with the debug logger on. The 96 KB in the summary is carried over from the proposal, and 5.5 flags it as possibly from the older run. So 112 KB is what I'd stand behind, pending the re-measure with logging off.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: So how would you fix that next time?
conversation: EXAMINER (heard): Let me push on the design. The clinics volunteered, didn't they? So you've got the keen ones in both arms, the staff knew which arm they were in, and nobody was blinded. How much of that six and a half point gap do you actually trust?

NATIVELY: You're right that the design has real limits, and the summary says so: clinics volunteered, staff and patients weren't blinded, and only 14 clinics were randomised. So I'd treat the 6.5 points as the estimate from this pilot, not a clean causal effect. The adjusted odds ratio was 1.41, with a wide confidence interval, 1.12 to 1.77, and the next step is randomising from all 31 district clinics.
items.answer: The fixes are already in the next steps: randomise from all 31 district clinics rather than the 14 that volunteered, run for 12 months instead of 12 weeks, and test the 48-hour and 3-hour reminders as separate arms so we can tell which one is doing the work. Blinding is harder at clinic level, but recruiting from the full district would at least cut the volunteer bias.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Right. General question then: why bother with a held-out test set at all when you could just cross-validate everything?
conversation: EXAMINER: Is the projector okay for people at the back? Can everyone read the axis labels?
USER (spoken): I can make the slides bigger if that helps.
EXAMINER: No, it's fine. And coffee is at half ten, by the way.
items.answer: Cross-validation gives you a better estimate of how the model performs, but it's still an estimate built from the same data you used to make choices. Every time you compare models, tune a hyperparameter, or pick a feature based on the cross-validated score, information from those folds leaks into your decisions, so the number gets quietly optimistic. A held-out test set stays untouched through all of that, so it's the one estimate that hasn't been shaped by your choices. That's why I keep it separate and only look at it at the end.

That's measured per 1-second window, from feature input to posterior output, so it excludes the front-end 40-band log-mel extraction, which wasn't timed separately. items.answer: Thanks for the introduction. I'm here to present my work, and I'll keep the background brief so we can get to the substance. My focus has been on the problem this thesis addresses, and the approach I've taken to it. I'll let the slides carry the detail, and I'm happy to go deeper on any part of it during questions.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Honestly, how does this stack up against quantization-aware training? That's what anyone deploying on a microcontroller would reach for first. Did you try it, and if not, why should we believe distillation is the better route?
items.answer: No, I didn't test quantization-aware training. My baselines are scratch training and standard KD, and the limitations section says so explicitly. The comparison I'm making is between training methods on the same 212k-parameter architecture, so QAT is orthogonal: it changes how the deployed model is represented, not how it's trained. STAGE-KD gives 93.2% against 91.8% for standard KD, at no on-device cost.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: If I only remember one thing from your talk, what should it be?
items.answer: If you remember one thing, make it this: the question I was asking matters more than any single result I showed. Everything in the talk was one attempt to answer it, and the useful part is that you can take the question away and test it against your own work.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: write me a thirty second thank-you to close, for the examiners and my supervisor, nothing cheesy
items.answer: Thanks for staying with me through the questions, and for the pushback on the method, it made the argument sharper. And to my supervisor, thank you for the steady guidance and for knowing when to let me work it out myself. I'm glad the work is in front of people who'll test it properly.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Which reminder did the work, the 48 hour one or the 3 hour one?
items.answer: We can't tell, and that's a real limitation of the design. Both reminders were always sent together, so the trial can't separate the 48-hour effect from the 3-hour one. That's exactly why the follow-on trial would test them as separate arms.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Five runs isn't many.
items.answer: Five seeds is what the thesis reports, and it's flagged as a limitation in section 5.6: five seeds limit how precisely we can estimate variance, and the ablations use three. That's also why the significance test in 5.3 is a paired bootstrap over test utterances with 10,000 resamples rather than a t-test across seeds, since five seeds give too few samples for a seed-level test to be informative. The difference against standard KD comes out at p < 0.01, though the bootstrap tests weren't corrected for multiple comparisons across the ablation variants.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What's your final accuracy, the number you're actually standing behind?
items.answer:
The number I'm standing behind is **94.1%** test accuracy, averaged over five seeds, with the 212k-parameter student. That's the figure in the summary paragraph of Chapter 5.

I should flag one thing honestly: the results table in section 5.2 currently shows 93.2% over three seeds, and my own notes say the summary may be from an older run and needs reconciling with the table. So 94.1% is what I'm claiming, but I'm still finishing the remaining seeds and will confirm the two match before I stand behind it as final.
